Lambek's syntactic calculus comprise the following rules:
x \to x
(xy) z \to x (yz)
x (y z) \to (xy) z
if xy \to z then x \to z/y
if xy \to z then y \to x \backslash z
if x \to z/y then xy \to z
if y \to x \backslash z then xy \to z
if x \to y and y \to z then x \to z
Put by Lambek: The system presented above may be viewed abstractly as a formal language with a number of primitive type symbols...
This description rings true, as we can read this as a very simple for type system for grammars that is later made more precise by Dougherty.

Define sequents x_1 , x_2 , \dots , x_n \to y to stand for ( \dots ((x_1 x_2) x_3) \dots x_n) \to y
x \to x
if T , y \to x then T \to x/y
if y , T \to x then T \to y \backslash x
if T \to y and U, x , V \to z then U , x/y , T , V \to z
if T \to y and U, x , V \to z then U , T, y \backslash x , V \to z
if U , x , y , V \to z then U , xy , V \to z
if P \to x and Q \to y then P, Q \to xy

If T \to x and U , x , V \to y then U , T , V \to y.
Gentzen's theorem shows that this rule does not increase the expressivity of the deductive system.

Fixing a set of base types B,
Typ is the set of type expressions generated from B over I, {} \multimap _L {}, {} \multimap _R {}
A lexicon is a set of entries of the from [ \alpha : a ], where \alpha is a lexical item and a \in Typ
A syntax tree is a binary tree whose leaves are lexical items
As phrase is a syntax tree with a linear ordering on its leaves

A syntax category over base types B and lexicon Lex is a closed category C that assigns an object \omega (b) to each b \in B, and a mapping \mu from Lex to arrows of C. That is, \mu (\alpha : a) : C[ 1 , \omega (\alpha ) ].

This work makes it more precise that closed monoidal categories form a natural setting for syntactic reasoning. However, it is perhaps still a little underwhelming and there is room for improvement. The correspondence to our ongoing work is:
Intuitively we can read Typ as giving the objects of a typing category
A lexicon behaves like a context with assignments to each variable. We may think of these assignments of variables to lexical items as giving sentence to be parsed
A syntax tree is a proof that the phrase given by the lexicon belongs to the grammar.
A semantic category is a closed category S such that there is a semantic functor F : C \to S that preserves the closed structure.
This notion is underwhelming, as it does not much insight into semantics nor does this paper give satisfying examples of semantics.

The only concrete example proposed by Dougherty give semantics in a presheaf category over a set of possible worlds. One of our insights is that by taking this to be presheaves over strings themselves, then we recover a universal semantics.
